analysis.one_liner: Ties federal police grants to use-of-force limits, de-escalation training, and civilian review boards.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2020 during the national debate over police violence, the bill attracted zero cosponsors and died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make states and cities ineligible for certain federal Justice Department law enforcement grants unless they adopt minimum use-of-force standards, create civilian-led review boards for deadly-force incidents, revoke the certifications of officers who seriously injure or kill people in violation of policy, and train officers in de-escalation and mental health crisis response. It would also require public disclosure of use-of-force policies and records, and direct the FBI to plan a national academy for local police.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities where police use force — the bill targets excessive and deadly force, requires independent review boards with a civilian majority, unseals officer discipline and use-of-force records, and pushes departments toward de-escalation and mental health crisis response instead of arrests.

how_it_helps.text: Conditions federal Byrne justice-assistance grant money on states and cities adopting minimum use-of-force standards, including limiting deadly force to imminent threats, banning chokeholds from the definition of acceptable force categories, and requiring officers to intervene when they see a policy violation.

Requires each grant recipient to create a review board for deadly-force incidents where a majority of members are not current or former law enforcement, with subpoena power and public written dispositions.
Requires grant recipients to revoke the certification of any officer found responsible for causing death or serious injury in violation of use-of-force standards.

Requires at least 16 hours of annual de-escalation and mental health crisis training for every officer, and directs that at least 10 percent of grant-supported salaries go to behavioral health specialists, reentry specialists, and public defenders.
Requires grant recipients to unseal records and policies that shield officer use-of-force and disciplinary information from public view, and to post their use-of-force policies publicly.

analysis.who_pays: State and local police agencies, which would face cuts of 25 to 50 percent of their Byrne grant funds if they do not adopt the required policies and training, and would give up some autonomy over officer discipline and use-of-force rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill enforces everything through federal grant conditions rather than direct law: the penalty for noncompliance on training is a 25 to 50 percent cut in Byrne grant funds, meaning a noncompliant department keeps most of its money and the consequence falls partly on the community's public safety budget.
The Attorney General can grant blanket exemptions from the review board and decertification requirements for 12 months, renewable once, delaying the reforms for two years after passage.
Review boards are capped at five members and their subpoena power exists only 'consistent with governing law,' so states with strong police protections could limit what a board can actually compel.

The bill's own findings concede that national police training is 'largely focused upon operational, investigatory, and tactical concerns' — a training-and-standards approach addresses conduct after departments adopt policies, but does not itself end qualified immunity or change the laws shielding officers from lawsuits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reforms are real but soft: they use the lever of federal grant money to push states toward civilian review boards, officer decertification, and de-escalation training, while leaving exemptions, Attorney General discretion, and partial funding cuts as escape valves. A supporter would call it a workable national floor; a skeptic would note that a department that keeps 60 to 75 percent of its grant money while refusing to reform has not been forced to do anything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cedric Richmond introduced the bill on June 8, 2020, during the national protest wave over police violence.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action was ever taken.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, from either party.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local law enforcement agencies are better off: they kept their federal Byrne grant money without having to adopt civilian review boards, officer decertification, minimum use-of-force standards, or public disclosure of disciplinary records.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that kept grant money without conditions

for.name: Rep. Cedric Richmond
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended

against.name: The 435 members of the House
against.what_they_did: None of them — 231 Democrats, 1 Independent, or 197 Republicans — signed on as a cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor but zero cosponsors of either party, so it never developed a partisan profile — no bloc, including the sponsor's own 231 House Democrats, endorsed it.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill conditions their federal Byrne grant money on minimum use-of-force standards, civilian-majority review boards, officer decertification, de-escalation training, and public disclosure of disciplinary and use-of-force records — with funding cuts of 25 to 50 percent for noncompliance. Departments that resisted these conditions kept the money because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Police unions and officer associations (Fraternal Order of Police, National Sheriffs' Association, etc.)
industries.note: The bill would remove officers from the majority of deadly-force review boards, strip certifications from officers found responsible for serious violations, and unseal records that shield officer discipline from public view — all areas where officer associations typically defend the status quo.

The bill requires crisis intervention training, contemplates mobile crisis teams and co-responder models, and directs at least 10 percent of grant salary support to behavioral health specialists and public defenders — routing new public funding toward non-police crisis response.

industries.industry: Federal Bureau of Investigation and federal police training institutions
industries.note: The bill directs the FBI to train state 'resource officers' every two years and to develop a plan for a 90-day residential National Law Enforcement Academy for local police, expanding the federal role in local police training.
